body:
So it looks like the documentation for the ElementRef is _incorrect_ as Renderer2 does _not_ provide any additional security - it is equivalent to the direct DOM manipulation in this regard. 

We should update docs to reflect this.

Indeed, Angular's [DefaultDomRenderer2](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/14.1.2/packages/platform-browser/src/dom/dom_renderer.ts#L137) is just a wrapper around DOM APIs, so it is as secure as these.

E.g. the example calls to `Renderer2` methods that I've shown in the issue description are likely not secure. But `Renderer2` can be used in a secure manner, when passing the right arguments to these methods. On the other hand, some other methods are always secure, no matter what arguments you feed to them. E.g. `createElement`, `createText`, `addClass`, `removeChild`, etc.

But these thoughts are specific `DefaultDomRenderer2`. Afaik there are scenarios where developers are expected to plug in their own implementation of `Renderer2`. So imho documentation of each Renderer2 method should state both of the following:

1. What secure behavior callers of the method can expect from any `Renderer2` implementation.
2. What secure behavior implementors of any `Renderer2` method must guarantee.

Now that I'm thinking about, these two are almost the same thing. Just viewed from a different angle.

I could attempt a PR for such documentation. But someone with more experience would need to review it carefully.

I see those things slightly differently: IMO we should _remove_ the mention of Renderer2 and security in the ElementRef documentation. And should indicate that Renderer2 has _no_ additional security guarantees (as compared to the regular DOM calls).

Sure, documenting that "Renderer2 has no additional security guarantees (as compared to the regular DOM calls)" seems fine.

But to be nitpicking, there isn't a one-to-one mapping between the methods of `Renderer2` and methods of the (HTML) DOM. E.g.:

* In DOM, you'd call `createElement` or `createElementNS` on a [Document](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document) node. 
In Angular there's just one such method, and you'd call it on the `Renderer2` itself.
* In DOM you'd call `appendChild` or `removeChild` on a [Node](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Node).
In Angular you'd call it on `Renderer2` itself and pass the target node as an argument. (Angular also does some special handling of `<template>` elements.)
* In DOM you'd call `setAttribute` and `removeAttribute` on an [Element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element).
In Angular you'd call it on `Renderer2` itself and pass the target node as an argument.
* In DOM you'd have to manipulate the `classList` property of an [Element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element) directly.
In Angular you'd call `addClass` or `removeClass` on the `Renderer2` and pass the target node as an argument.
* ...

I guess this mapping is fairly self-explanatory. But it might still be confusing to some people.

Besides I'm still confused myself about the relationship between _DOM_ and _Renderer2_. The docs of the latter say:

> Extend this base class to implement custom rendering. By default, Angular renders a template into DOM. You can use custom rendering to intercept rendering calls, or to render to something other than DOM.

Wouldn't that include rendering that has nothing to do with the DOM or even HTML/SVG/MathML/etc at all?

I really cannot think of a meaningful scenario for this. Maybe something weird, like rendering an Angular application directly into a tree of gtk widgets? If this were a valid case, comparison to DOM wouldn't be very helpful.

@pkozlowski-opensource @meeque 

From what I see in the code the Renderer2 methods are only more secure because we have the wrapping Renderer2 methods over the native DOM methods so it might be a bit more “secure” because we don’t access the DOM element directly but that’s it.

I would mention in the docs that Sanitizer/DomSanitizer should be used if we actually want to scan the code for security problems.

What do you say?

Update:

I opened this PR in hope to resolve this issue:
https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/51207

- [ ] angular.io application / infrastructure changes
- [ ] Other... Please describe:


## What is the current behavior?
Related to: https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/46904

In the current state, the documentation suggests that usage of `Renderer2` provides a safe way to access DOM elements. It only provides a wrapper method around it thus we are not using DOM API directly when coding, which is fine, but doesn't provide any additional security so it might be confusing. (to me it was until I checked the source code and saw that I also need to use `.sanitize()` for security benefits)

Sorry if I misunderstood something.

Issue Number: N/A


## What is the new behavior?
I mentioned the `DomSanitizer` so that it is a bit more clear that using `Renderer2` isn't enough by itself but for maximum security but that it should be used in combination with the `DomSanitizer`.

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

body:
@meeque I fully agree with you that the Renderer2 needs better documentation.
I quote from your comment:

> "On the other hand, some other methods are always secure, no matter what arguments you feed to them. E.g. createElement, createText, addClass, removeChild, etc."

I just found that out, since I was sanitizing content before passing it to the `createText` method resulting in html entities inside my output. Isn't this supposed to be mentioned somewhere?
Would it not be a good idea to just write in the comment for each method whether it needs sanitizing of unsafe content or whether it is safe to use without sanitization!

i.e. I would not dare to use `addClass` without sanitizing since documentation claiming it is safe to do so is missing...
